opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we spend a lot of time on, because the gap between "a robot can do this in a demo" and "a robot can do this eight hours a day in a real facility" is enormous.

The first filter for me is whether the task is structured enough that you can define success clearly, but variable enough that classical automation hasn't already solved it. If something is perfectly repetitive, a fixed industrial arm on a conveyor does it better and cheaper than any general-purpose robot ever will. The interesting middle ground is tasks with some variation: objects aren't always in the same place, the environment changes a bit, maybe you have to walk somewhere, pick something up, and put it somewhere else. Today that's mostly done by people, and the ROI of automating it with traditional methods just isn't there.

The second filter is tolerance for imperfection. In the near term these systems won't be 100% reliable, so you want tasks where a failure is cheap and recoverable. If the robot drops a box, it can try again or call for help. You don't want to start somewhere a mistake damages expensive equipment or puts someone at risk.

Third, and this comes from my background in reinforcement learning and simulation, I ask how much of the task we can learn in simulation versus how much needs real-world data. Locomotion transfers really well from sim to real now; we've seen that over the last several years with legged robots. Contact-rich manipulation with deformable objects or tight tolerances is much harder to simulate. So near term, I'd favor tasks that lean on robust locomotion and fairly coarse manipulation: moving totes, loading and unloading, carrying parts between stations. Fine dexterous assembly is further out.

Finally, there's a very practical layer: can you deploy without redesigning the customer's facility? A big appeal of more general, mobile robots is that they fit into spaces built for humans. If a task requires the customer to re-engineer their whole line, it isn't really a near-term task, whatever the robot can technically do.

So it's the overlap of all of that: enough variability to need intelligence, forgiving enough to tolerate today's reliability, learnable with the tools we have, and deployable into existing environments. That overlap is smaller than the hype suggests, but it's real, and I think it grows quickly once you're in the field collecting data.

r001.rationale: The response recommends starting with near-term tasks involving robust locomotion and coarse manipulation, such as moving totes and carrying parts, while placing fine dexterous assembly further out.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that the question of which tasks is almost more important than the question of which algorithms, at least right now. Coming from the research side, you get used to picking problems because they're interesting or because they push some capability, and in industry it's kind of the opposite. You start from what actually has value and then work backwards to what's feasible.

The way I think about it, there are a few criteria. The first one is how much variability there really is in the task. A lot of industrial work looks repetitive from the outside, but when you actually go and look at it, there's a surprising amount of variation, in the objects, in where things are placed, in the lighting, in what a person did before the robot arrived. The sweet spot for the near term is tasks that have enough variability that classical automation doesn't work, otherwise someone would have already automated it with a fixed setup, but not so much that you need something close to general intelligence to handle it. So things like moving boxes, loading and unloading, some kinds of inspection, that middle band.

The second thing is the cost of failure. If the robot drops a box, that's usually fine. If the robot drops something fragile or expensive, or if a failure means a line stops for an hour, that completely changes what reliability you need. And reliability is really the hard part. Getting a demo to ninety percent is one thing, getting to the level where someone will actually trust it in their facility overnight is a very different thing. So I tend to look for tasks where occasional failure is recoverable, where a human can step in, or where the robot can just try again.

The third one, which I think is underestimated, is how much you can reshape the environment. Pure research tends to say the robot has to deal with the world as it is. In practice, if you can agree with the customer on some small constraints, like where the pallets go or what kind of containers are used, that can make an otherwise very hard problem quite tractable. It's not cheating, it's engineering. The question is just how much you can ask before it becomes a different process for them.

And then honestly the last factor is data and iteration speed. For the kind of learning-based approaches we work with, you want a task where you can simulate it reasonably well, or where you can collect a lot of experience quickly, and where you can deploy, see what breaks, and go back and fix it in a tight loop. Tasks where every iteration takes weeks are much harder to make progress on, regardless of how good the method is.

So when I put all of that together, the near-term picture is a lot of logistics and material handling, things in warehouses and factories that are physically demanding and kind of unpleasant for people, with moderate variability and forgiving failure modes. That's where I think legged and mobile manipulation systems can actually earn their place first, and then you expand from there as the reliability and the generality improve.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes near-term tasks with moderate variability and manageable failure modes, such as logistics and material handling, as the starting point before expanding to harder tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with the task, rather than with the robot. What does the robot actually need to do, and how much variability is there? Something that looks very simple to a person can be quite difficult for a robot if the objects are different every time, or if it requires delicate contact and recovering from mistakes.

So, in the near term, I would look for tasks where you can constrain the environment, where the motion or manipulation is relatively repetitive, and where there’s a clear benefit from automation. You also have to look beyond a successful demonstration. Can it run reliably for an entire shift? What happens when it fails? Can someone intervene easily?

That doesn’t necessarily mean automating an entire job. It might mean taking one particularly repetitive or physically demanding part of a workflow and doing that well. I think that’s a much more practical starting point, and then you can expand as the capabilities improve.

r001.rationale: The response recommends starting with constrained, repetitive tasks or one repetitive part of a workflow, presenting that as the practical near-term approach to robot deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to look at the whole task, rather than just asking whether the robot can perform a particular motion. How predictable is the environment? What objects does it need to interact with? What happens if it makes a mistake? And how often does someone need to step in?

For the near term, I would look for tasks that are repetitive, physically demanding, and relatively well structured. You want enough variability that using a robot makes sense, but you also want to be able to define and test the conditions it will encounter. Moving something between known locations is a much more manageable starting point than asking a robot to do whatever a person does throughout a factory.

And then there's the practical question: does it actually help? A demonstration can look very impressive, but if the system needs constant supervision, or takes too long to recover from a failure, it may not be useful. So I think the right starting point is a narrow task where you can achieve reliable operation and provide a clear benefit, and then expand from there.

r001.rationale: It recommends starting with narrow, repetitive, well-structured tasks and expanding from there.
